unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 3: Life in the Wild! In this unit, you will explore the natural world through the lens of East African ecosystems. You will discover how animals, plants, and their environments are connected in amazing ways. Every living thing depends on something else to survive, and understanding these connections helps us take better care of the world around us.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and vocabulary. Read and annotate the source texts. Discuss evidence and language choices. Apply the grammar focus. Draft and revise two to three paragraphs. Present, reflect and complete the quiz.

visual.alt: Learners investigating ecosystems and evidence from the natural world

readings.title: Life in the Wild: source text 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
East Africa is a region which stretches from the dry plains of Somalia to the green highlands of Ethiopia and the vast savannahs of Kenya and Tanzania. It is home to one of the richest collections of wildlife on Earth. Every animal, plant, and insect plays a part in the great web of life. Scientists call this web an ecosystem — a community of living things that depend on each other and on the land, water, and air around them.
At the heart of every ecosystem lies the food chain. A food chain shows who eats whom. It begins with plants, which use sunlight and carbon dioxide to make their own food through a process called photosynthesis. These plants are called producers because they produce the energy that the entire chain depends on. In the semi-arid grasslands of the Horn of Africa, tough grasses and thorny acacia trees are the main producers. They endure months of dry heat and burst into life when the rains finally come, feeding the animals that graze across the plains.
Understanding this web begins with a few important words. A habitat is the natural home of an animal or plant, and a species is a group of living things of the same kind. Some creatures are predators, which hunt other animals for food, while their prey are the animals that are hunted. As you read the passages in this unit, watch for these words, and notice how each writer uses the present simple tense to state facts that are always true. Notice, too, the relative clauses — small groups of words beginning with who, which, or where — that add extra detail about the animals and places being described.
The natural world of East Africa is both beautiful and fragile. Every grassland, river, and coral reef depends on a careful balance, and that balance is easier to break than it looks. When one species disappears, the animals that depend on it can suffer too, and the effects can spread right along the food chain. As you learn how food chains and ecosystems work, you will also discover why protecting them matters for every family and community that shares the land, water, and air of this remarkable region.

readings.title: Life in the Wild: source text 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
At the heart of every ecosystem lies the food chain. A food chain shows who eats whom. It begins with plants, which use sunlight and carbon dioxide to make their own food through a process called photosynthesis. These plants are called producers because they produce energy for the entire chain. In the semi-arid grasslands of the Horn of Africa, tough grasses and thorny acacia trees are the main producers. They endure months of dry heat and burst into life when the rains finally come.
The next link in the chain is the herbivore — an animal that eats only plants. On the East African savannah, herds of zebra, wildebeest, and gazelle graze on the grasslands. In the drier regions near Somali towns, the camel — which people sometimes call the “ship of the desert” — feeds on dry shrubs and thorny branches that other animals cannot reach. The gerenuk, a slender antelope which is found in Somalia and Kenya, stands on its hind legs to browse the highest leaves. Each herbivore has its own habitat and its own way of surviving.
Then come the predators — the meat-eaters who hunt other animals for food. The lion, which lives in family groups called prides, is one of East Africa’s most famous predators. Cheetahs, who are the fastest land animals on Earth, chase gazelle across the open plains. The Somali wild dog hunts in packs, working together to catch prey that is larger than any single dog. High above, eagles and vultures circle the sky, watching for small mammals and reptiles below. These birds of prey play an important role because they clean the environment by eating dead animals.
Water creates its own chain. Along the rivers and seasonal pools, frogs and toads are common. These amphibians — animals that live both in water and on land — eat insects and are in turn eaten by snakes and herons. Off the coast of East Africa, the coral reefs are underwater ecosystems where thousands of species of fish, crabs, and sea turtles find food and shelter. Whale sharks, which are the largest fish in the ocean, visit these warm waters to feed on tiny plankton.
Every part of this web matters. Remove one species, and the whole chain can fall apart. When farmers clear land for crops, they destroy the habitat of wild animals. When hunters kill too many predators, the number of herbivores grows too large, and they eat all the grass until the land turns to dust. When plastic waste reaches the ocean, it becomes a threat to sea turtles who mistake it for jellyfish. The balance of nature is treacherous — it can look strong, but it is easily broken.

readings.title: The Red Cloth, part 1
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
The sun rose slowly over the hills of Kalembo, a village surrounded by dust and silence. Three months ago, everything had changed.
Foreign soldiers had arrived. They wore sharp grey coats and marched in tight rows. Without warning, they had proclaimed that Kalembo now belonged to a land “across the sea.” No one had seen this ruler. People called him a dictator, someone who gave orders no one could question.
The soldiers took control of the grain stores. They set up new laws in an administration centre — a stone building filled with papers and stamps. “This is what they call bureaucracy,” said the village elder. “A system where rules matter more than people.”
Twelve-year-old Amal had lived in Kalembo her whole life. She remembered laughter, music, and baskets of mangoes under the fig tree. Now she heard orders barked in a language she did not understand. People whispered more than they spoke, and soldiers watched every corner.
One day, a funeral was held for an old farmer who had refused to hand over his harvest. He had died quietly in his sleep, some said from starvation. A crowd gathered beside the river to mourn and bury him. Women wore shawls, men stood in silence, and children held hands.
Suddenly, a group of soldiers arrived. “No gatherings allowed!” one of them shouted. “This is a prohibited event.”
“But it is a funeral,” someone said.
“All events must be approved,” said the soldier. “Even grief must follow rules.”
The villagers dispersed slowly, heads bowed. But something stayed — an emotion deeper than sorrow. Frustration. Amal stood beside her mother and whispered, “They fear even our tears.”
That night, Amal asked her grandfather, “Why do they treat us this way?”
“Because people who oppress others are afraid,” he said. “They fear what they cannot control — memory, belief, unity.” She did not fully understand, but she remembered his words.
The next day, the soldiers painted warnings on walls: “Anyone who refuses to obey will be treated as treacherous.” The words were meant to scare, but they lit a fire in Amal’s heart. “These words,” she told her friend Leo, “are like weapons.”
“Then we need words too,” he said.
That night, they gathered red cloth scraps — bright, crimson, the colour the old farmer had worn when he walked through town. Amal’s mother had once called it “a colour no fear can hide.” Amal, Leo, and others tied the cloths on trees, water pots, and rooftops. On fences, they painted messages in charcoal: “This land has roots.” “We are people, not property.” They did not sign the messages, but the whole vicinity began to feel different. A wind of quiet courage blew through the village.

readings.title: The Red Cloth, part 2
readings.setting: East African and familiar learner contexts
readings.passageScript:
When the soldiers saw the red cloths, they grew angry. “Who is behind this?” they shouted. “These symbols are treacherous.” But no one spoke. It was a collective silence, and the villagers had found power in not revealing the truth.
The next day, all the cloths were torn down. But by sunset, new ones had appeared. At school, the teacher gave a new writing assignment: “Choose someone who showed courage. Write how they faced hardship, and how they responded.”
Amal wrote about her grandmother, who had once hidden refugees fleeing the war. “She was quiet,” Amal wrote, “but she acted. That is strength.” Leo wrote about a man named Kofi, an abolitionist who had fought slavery through song and secret messages.
Others wrote about leaders from the past. They used relative clauses naturally: “My grandmother, who raised me, believed in truth.” “Kofi, whose words became songs, never gave up.” “A soldier is someone who follows orders, which can destroy or protect.”
One morning, the soldiers arrived at school. “These books,” they said, “contain propaganda.” They burned several. “You must only learn what we allow.” Amal looked down, but something inside her refused to shrink.
That week, there were whispers of sickness. A health worker arrived from the capital to test the water. “This is a case of typhoid,” she said. “It is caused by unsafe drinking water.” She handed out carbon filters and gave instructions. “Boil your water. Avoid contaminated streams. Illness is not always observable. It hides.”
Later, Amal told Leo, “Injustice is like typhoid. You do not always see it, but it poisons everything.”
As the months passed, small changes grew. The soldiers patrolled less and shouted less. A new rule appeared: “You may bury your dead in groups of five or fewer.” “It is not freedom,” someone muttered, “but it is a crack in the wall.” Amal’s grandfather said, “It shows they feel pressure. They see we endure.”
The teacher asked the class to reflect: “What happens when people face power they cannot fight?” Amal raised her hand. “Some plant roots. Quiet ones. Ones that reach deep.” The crimson cloths returned, not just as symbols but in clothes, art, and flags.
One day, years later, a traveller came to Kalembo. He had heard of the red cloths, and he asked the villagers, “Who started the movement?” Amal, now older, pointed to a grave wrapped in crimson. “The man we buried,” she said. She pointed to a tree with painted bark. “The questions we asked.” Then she smiled. “And the girl I once was.”

comprehension.question: What is an ecosystem? Explain it in your own words.
comprehension.correctAnswer: An ecosystem is a community of living things and their surroundings — the land, water and air — all connected and depending on one another.
comprehension.explanation: Paragraph one defines an ecosystem as a community of living things that depend on each other and on the land, water and air around them.

comprehension.question: Name two herbivores from the passage and say what each one eats.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Zebra, wildebeest and gazelle are herbivores that graze on the savannah grasslands, while the camel feeds on dry shrubs and thorny branches other animals cannot reach.
comprehension.explanation: The passage lists several grazing herbivores and describes the camel eating dry shrubs; accept any two with what they eat.

comprehension.question: Why did the soldiers stop the old farmer’s funeral?
comprehension.correctAnswer: The soldiers said no gatherings were allowed and that the funeral was a prohibited event, because every event now had to be approved first.
comprehension.explanation: In the story the soldiers declare the funeral a prohibited event and insist that all events, even grief, must follow their rules.

comprehension.question: What reason did the soldiers give for burning the school books?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They claimed the books contained propaganda and said the villagers must only learn what the soldiers allowed.
comprehension.explanation: In part two the soldiers call the books propaganda and burn several, telling the villagers to learn only what is permitted.

comprehension.question: Why does the passage call plants the “producers” of a food chain?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Plants are called producers because they use sunlight and carbon dioxide to make their own food through photosynthesis, producing the energy the whole chain depends on.
comprehension.explanation: The text explains that plants begin the food chain and produce energy for the entire chain, which is why they are named producers.

comprehension.question: According to the passage, why are eagles and vultures important to the ecosystem?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They clean the environment by eating dead animals, which helps stop disease from spreading and keeps the food web healthy.
comprehension.explanation: The text states that these birds of prey play an important role because they clean the environment by eating dead animals.

comprehension.question: What did Amal and Leo do with the red cloth, and why did they choose that colour?
comprehension.correctAnswer: They tied crimson red-cloth scraps to trees, water pots and rooftops as a quiet symbol of resistance, choosing red because it was the colour the old farmer had worn — “a colour no fear can hide.”
comprehension.explanation: The passage describes the children tying red cloths around the village and links the crimson colour to the farmer and to courage.

comprehension.question: The health worker says, “Illness is not always observable.” How does Amal later connect this idea to injustice?
comprehension.correctAnswer: Amal says injustice is like typhoid — you do not always see it, but it poisons everything — comparing the hidden illness in the water to the hidden harm of unfair rule.
comprehension.explanation: The answer should link the observable/hidden illness to Amal’s simile that injustice quietly poisons everything.

comprehension.question: The passage says acacia trees and tough grasses “endure months of dry heat.” Explain how this helps them survive in the Horn of Africa.
comprehension.correctAnswer: Because they endure the long dry season and then burst into life when the rains come, these producers survive the harsh, semi-arid climate and keep feeding the animals that graze the plains.
comprehension.explanation: A strong answer links the word endure to survival: the producers wait out the drought and revive with the rains, so the food chain continues.

comprehension.question: The passage says, “Remove one species, and the whole chain can fall apart.” Use an example from the text to explain what can happen when the balance is broken.
comprehension.correctAnswer: When hunters kill too many predators, the herbivores grow too many and eat all the grass until the land turns to dust, showing how one change can break the whole treacherous balance of nature.
comprehension.explanation: A strong answer quotes or paraphrases a text example — over-hunting predators, clearing habitat, or ocean plastic — to show one change damaging the whole chain.

comprehension.question: Amal’s grandfather says, “people who oppress others are afraid.” What do you think he means?
comprehension.correctAnswer: He means that those who oppress others fear what they cannot control — memory, belief and unity — so they use harsh rules to hide their own fear; answers should explain this idea in the learner’s own words.
comprehension.explanation: This is an inference question; a good response connects the grandfather’s words to the soldiers’ fear of things they cannot control.

comprehension.question: At the end, Amal names three things that started the movement: the man they buried, the questions they asked, and the girl she was. Why does she name all three?
comprehension.correctAnswer: She names all three to show the movement grew from many small acts — one person’s courage, the community’s questions and her own choices — rather than from a single leader, which is the story’s message that truth finds many ways to speak.
comprehension.explanation: A strong answer connects the three images to the theme that quiet, shared resistance, not one hero, changed the village.

grammar.title: The Present Simple Tense — Stating Facts
grammar.explanation: We use the present simple tense for facts, habits and things that are always or generally true. When we write about animals, ecosystems and food chains, this tense states information clearly and accurately.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Form the present simple from the base verb. For I, you, we and they, use the base form: “Lions hunt in groups.” For he, she and it, add -s or -es: “A cheetah runs very fast.” Verbs ending in -s, -sh, -ch, -x or -o add -es (watch → watches, go → goes), and verbs ending in a consonant plus y change to -ies (fly → flies). To make a negative, use do not or does not with the base verb: “Herbivores do not eat meat.” To ask a question, begin with Do or Does: “Does the whale shark eat fish?” Example facts: “Cheetahs run faster than any other land animal.” “Plants produce energy through photosynthesis.”
grammar.commonMistake: A frequent error is dropping the -s for he, she or it, writing “The eagle fly high” instead of “The eagle flies high.”
grammar.memoryTip: Ask yourself, “Is this always true?” If it is, keep the verb in the present simple.
grammar.practice:
Part A: choose the correct verb form. A vulture (clean / cleans) the environment; frogs (live / lives) in water and on land; the gerenuk (stand / stands) on its hind legs. Part B: write two facts of your own about East African animals using the present simple.

Answer key (self-check):
Part A — a vulture cleans the environment (singular subject, add -s); frogs live in water and on land (plural subject, base form); the gerenuk stands on its hind legs (singular subject, add -s).
Part B (open-ended — model example, not a fixed answer): any two generally-true facts in the present simple are correct, e.g. “Giraffes eat leaves from tall acacia trees.” “Elephants live together in family groups.” Check that you used the base verb for plural or I/you/we/they subjects, and added -s or -es for a singular he/she/it subject.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Present Simple — The Verb 'to be' for Facts
grammar.explanation: The verb to be — am, is and are — describes what something is, classifies it and states facts about identity and character. It is one of the most useful verbs when we write about the natural world.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Match the verb to its subject. I take am: “I am a student.” He, she and it take is: “The cheetah is the fastest land animal.” You, we and they take are: “Coral reefs are underwater ecosystems.” Make a negative by adding not, or use the contractions isn’t and aren’t: “A whale shark is not a whale; it is a fish.” To ask a question, put the verb before the subject: “Is the gerenuk an antelope?” “Are amphibians cold-blooded?” More facts: “The Somali wild ass is one of the most endangered animals in the world.” “Frogs are amphibians.”
grammar.commonMistake: Watch subject–verb agreement: “The elephants is large” should be “The elephants are large,” and “The lion are a predator” should be “The lion is a predator.”
grammar.memoryTip: One thing takes is; more than one thing takes are.
grammar.practice:
Part A: fill each gap with is, are, isn’t or aren’t. The African elephant ___ the largest land animal; frogs ___ mammals, they ___ amphibians. Part B: write two true sentences about coral reefs using the verb to be.

Answer key (self-check):
Part A — The African elephant is the largest land animal; frogs aren’t mammals, they are amphibians.
Part B (open-ended — model example, not a fixed answer): any two true sentences about coral reefs using is/are are correct, e.g. “Coral reefs are underwater ecosystems.” “A coral reef is home to thousands of fish species.” Check that you matched is to a singular subject and are to a plural subject.

grammar.title: Relative Clauses with 'who' (for people)
grammar.explanation: A relative clause gives extra information about a noun. We use who when the noun is a person, telling the reader what that person does, believes or is like, and joining two short ideas into one detailed sentence.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Begin with a sentence about a person, then add a clause starting with who: “Scientists study ecosystems” and “Scientists are called ecologists” become “Scientists who study ecosystems are called ecologists.” More examples: “The ranger who protects the park is called Talia.” “Farmers who clear forests destroy animal habitats.” A defining clause tells us exactly which person and takes no commas: “The girl who won the race is my friend.” A non-defining clause adds extra detail and uses commas: “Amal, who was only twelve, showed great courage.”
grammar.commonMistake: Do not use which for people: “The teacher which helped us” should be “The teacher who helped us.”
grammar.memoryTip: If you can swap the word for a person’s name, who is the right choice.
grammar.practice:
Part A: join each pair with who. The ranger protects wild animals. She works in a national park. Part B: write one sentence about a scientist and one about a farmer, each using a who clause.

Answer key (self-check):
Part A — The ranger who protects wild animals works in a national park. (Reordering it as “The ranger, who works in a national park, protects wild animals.” is also correct.)
Part B (open-ended — model example, not a fixed answer): follow the pattern from the rule above, e.g. “Scientists who study ecosystems are called ecologists.” and “Farmers who clear forests destroy animal habitats.” Check that you used who, not which, because both sentences are about people.
grammar.reviewStatus: Needs re-review (content updated for self-sufficiency pass)

grammar.title: Relative Clauses with 'which' and 'that' (for animals and things)
grammar.explanation: We use which for animals, things and ideas, never for people, and we can also use that in defining clauses. Both let us add important detail to sentences about the natural world.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Start with a sentence about an animal or thing, then add a clause with which or that: “The coral reef provides shelter” and “The coral reef is underwater” become “The coral reef, which is underwater, provides shelter.” Use that in a defining clause with no commas: “The animal that eats only plants is called a herbivore.” Use which in a non-defining clause with commas to add extra detail: “The elephant, which is the largest land animal, lives in family groups.” More examples: “The camel, which can survive without water for days, is found across East Africa.” “The lion, which lives in prides, is a famous predator.”
grammar.commonMistake: Do not use who for things: “The tree who grows near the river” should be “The tree which grows near the river.” For animals, which or that is the safe choice; writers sometimes use who for animals they treat as characters (the source text has “Cheetahs, who are the fastest land animals”), but a thing never takes who.
grammar.memoryTip: For a creature or a thing — anything that is not a person — reach for which or that, never who.
grammar.practice:
Part A: fill each gap with which or that, adding commas where a clause is non-defining. The cheetah is a predator ___ runs faster than any other land animal. Part B: write two sentences about East African animals, each using a which or that clause.

Answer key (self-check):
Part A — The cheetah is a predator that runs faster than any other land animal. (No commas: this is a defining clause that tells us exactly which predator.)
Part B (open-ended — model example, not a fixed answer): any two sentences about East African animals with which or that are correct, e.g. “The camel, which can survive without water for days, is found across East Africa.” “The animal that eats only plants is called a herbivore.” Check for commas around a non-defining which clause, and no commas around a defining that clause.

grammar.title: Relative Clauses with 'where' (for places)
grammar.explanation: We use where when the noun is a place. A relative clause with where tells the reader what happens at a location or why it matters, which is especially useful for describing habitats and ecosystems.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Start with a sentence about a place, then add a clause with where: “The savannah is a grassland” and “Many animals graze on the savannah” become “The savannah is a grassland where many animals graze.” More examples: “Coral reefs are underwater ecosystems where thousands of species find food and shelter.” “The national park is a protected area where no hunting is allowed.” You can still use which for a place when it is the subject: “The park, which is very large, has many animals”; but when you mean in that place, use where: “The park where many animals live is protected.”
grammar.commonMistake: Use where for a location, not which: say “the park where we play,” not “the park which we play.”
grammar.memoryTip: If you can replace the word with “in that place,” then where is correct.
grammar.practice:
Part A: complete each sentence with where and your own ending. The Serengeti is a grassland where ___. The coral reef is a habitat where ___. Part B: describe your local area in one sentence using a where clause.

Answer key (self-check):
Part A (open-ended — model example, not a fixed answer): any true, sensible ending works, e.g. “The Serengeti is a grassland where zebras and wildebeest graze during the migration.” “The coral reef is a habitat where colourful fish shelter among the coral.”
Part B (open-ended — model example, not a fixed answer): any sentence naming your area and using where is correct, e.g. “My neighbourhood is a place where children play football after school.” Check that where introduces a place and the clause explains what happens there.

grammar.title: Combining Present Simple with Relative Clauses
grammar.explanation: The real power of grammar appears when we combine the present simple with relative clauses, building rich, factual sentences about the natural world for a research report or a Cambridge assessment.
grammar.ruleAndExamples: Use the present simple for the main fact and add a relative clause for detail: “The cheetah, which is the fastest land animal, hunts gazelles on the open plains.” “Ecologists are scientists who study how living things interact with their environment.” “The savannah is a grassland where zebras, wildebeest and gazelles graze.” Build in steps: begin with “The eagle hunts small mammals,” add detail to make “The eagle, which has excellent eyesight, hunts small mammals,” then add a place: “… in the savannah where tall grasses provide cover.”
grammar.commonMistake: When a relative clause sits in the middle of a sentence, do not forget the closing comma: “The eagle, which has sharp eyes hunts mice” needs a comma after “eyes.”
grammar.memoryTip: Build in stages: state the fact first, then add one relative clause for extra detail.
grammar.practice:
Part A: expand “The lion hunts zebra” by adding a which or where clause. Part B: write three factual sentences about East African wildlife, each in the present simple and each with at least one relative clause.

Answer key (self-check):
Part A (open-ended — model example, not a fixed answer): several expansions are correct, e.g. “The lion, which lives in a pride, hunts zebra.” or “The lion hunts zebra on the savannah where the grass grows tall.” Check that you added exactly one which/where clause, with commas if it is non-defining.
Part B (open-ended — model example, not a fixed answer): any three factual present-simple sentences with a relative clause are correct, e.g. “The cheetah, which is the fastest land animal, hunts gazelles on the open plains.” “Ecologists are scientists who study how living things interact with their environment.” “The savannah is a grassland where zebras, wildebeest and gazelles graze.”

writing.title: Writing 1: Animal Research Report
writing.promptAndInstructions: Plan and write a research report about one East African animal, such as the Somali wild ass, the gerenuk, the whale shark or the African elephant. Organise your report into clear paragraphs covering appearance, habitat, diet and food-chain position, survival and threats, and one surprising fact. Use the present simple tense for your facts and include at least three relative clauses with who, which or where.
writing.modelText: The African elephant is the largest land animal on Earth. It is a herbivore which lives in the savannahs and forests of East Africa, moving in family groups led by the oldest female, whom scientists call the matriarch. Elephants matter to the ecosystem because they spread seeds and open paths that other animals use.
writing.successCriteria: I answered the prompt; organised ideas into paragraphs; used precise Unit vocabulary; supported ideas with evidence; considered viewpoint where relevant; checked cohesion and punctuation; revised my work
writing.support: Plan a clear structure, topic sentences and supporting evidence, then use the word bank and source models.
writing.extension: Synthesize details from more than one text, vary sentence structures, improve transitions and strengthen the conclusion.

writing.title: Writing 2: Amal’s Diary Entry

quizzes.question: What does 'threat' mean?
quizzes.options: Something that can cause harm or danger. | A difficult situation that causes suffering or trouble. | A leader who has complete power and makes all the rules without asking others. | To treat someone in a cruel or unfair way, making them feel weak or powerless.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Something that can cause harm or danger.
quizzes.explanation: The dark clouds are a threat of a coming storm.

quizzes.question: What does 'treacherous' mean?
quizzes.options: A difficult situation that causes suffering or trouble. | Dangerous and not safe, often because it is not what it seems. | To treat someone badly or unfairly because of their beliefs or identity. | To treat someone in a cruel or unfair way, making them feel weak or powerless.
quizzes.correctAnswer: Dangerous and not safe, often because it is not what it seems.
quizzes.explanation: The path through the mountains was treacherous after the rains.

quizzes.question: What does 'dictator' mean?
quizzes.options: A difficult situation that causes suffering or trouble. | To say that something is not allowed. | A leader who has complete power and makes all the rules without asking others. | To treat someone badly or unfairly because of their beliefs or identity.
quizzes.correctAnswer: A leader who has complete power and makes all the rules without asking others.
quizzes.explanation: The dictator did not allow people to speak freely or choose their leaders.

quizzes.question: What does 'oppress' mean?
quizzes.options: To keep going through something difficult without giving up. | To say that something is not allowed. | To treat someone in a cruel or unfair way, making them feel weak or powerless. | To treat someone badly or unfairly because of their beliefs or identity.
quizzes.correctAnswer: To treat someone in a cruel or unfair way, making them feel weak or powerless.
quizzes.explanation: The soldiers tried to oppress the villagers by taking away their rights.

teacherNotes.note: Model new language aloud, check meaning before independent work, and vary response modes. An adult or caregiver should be present and supervise any recording or online activity. Give specific feedback on complete sentences, evidence from the text and precise use of unit vocabulary.

Point learners to their AI tutor for support drawn from the source files: reading the story aloud and explaining hard parts, checking a diary entry or animal report for grammar and vocabulary, quizzing them on the unit words, and helping them find and combine relative clauses with who, which and where.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Look for a chain of at least four correctly ordered links (producer, herbivore, predator, and top predator or scavenger), each labelled and described in a present-simple sentence with a relative clause, e.g. “The acacia tree is a producer which makes food using sunlight.”

1 False — a predator hunts other animals, it does not eat only plants. 2 True. 3 True. 4 False — “who” is for people and “which” is for things. 5 True. 6 False — camels are herbivores. 7 True. 8 False — a relative clause gives extra information about a noun, not a verb.
1 ecosystem, 2 habitat, 3 predator, 4 prey, 5 species, 6 crimson, 7 endure, 8 vicinity.

Accept any reasoned prediction that uses because and the present simple, e.g. if the lions disappear the zebra population rises and then over-grazes the grass; if a factory pollutes the river the frogs and fish die and the animals that eat them lose their food.
Look for a paragraph that compares two animals using the sentence starters, includes at least one relative clause, and ends by explaining why both animals matter to the ecosystem.

Accept any sensible sorting of twelve unit words into named groups (for example power-and-control words, community words and nature words), with the rule for each group explained in a complete sentence.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Something that can cause harm or danger. The dark clouds are a threat of a coming storm.
Dangerous and not safe, often because it is not what it seems. The path through the mountains was treacherous after the rains.
A leader who has complete power and makes all the rules without asking others. The dictator did not allow people to speak freely or choose their leaders.
To treat someone in a cruel or unfair way, making them feel weak or powerless. The soldiers tried to oppress the villagers by taking away their rights.
A difficult situation that causes suffering or trouble. After the drought, many families faced hardship because they lost their crops.
To treat someone badly or unfairly because of their beliefs or identity. It is wrong to persecute people just because they are different.
To say that something is not allowed. The soldiers tried to prohibit gatherings in the village.
To keep going through something difficult without giving up. The villagers had to endure months of harsh rules and limited food.
To say something loudly or officially. The leader proclaimed that the village now belonged to a foreign power.
A ceremony to remember and say goodbye to someone who has died. The whole community gathered at the funeral to honour the old farmer.
